ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The image shows a schematic diagram of a square floor paved with congruent small square tiles; the black tiles are located on the two diagonals from one corner to the opposite corner, and the remaining tiles are white. The center example also shows the two diagonals intersecting at the center of the square, with the center black tile counted only once. Reasoning: Suppose the square floor has n tiles on each side, then the total number of tiles is n^2. The two diagonals each have n black tiles. If n is odd, the two diagonals will overlap at the center tile, so the total number of black tiles is n+n-1=2n-1. The problem gives the number of black tiles as 101, and 101 is odd, so there should be 2n-1=101. Solving gives 2n=102, n=51. Therefore the total number of tiles is 51^2=2601.

method.method_draft: Let the floor have n tiles on each side, so the total number is n^2. From the image, the black tiles are exactly those lying on the two corner-to-corner diagonals, with the middle tile counted only once when the side length is odd. From the text, the number of black tiles is 101. Each diagonal contributes n black tiles; because 101 is odd, the two diagonals must overlap in one central tile, so 101 = n + n - 1 = 2n - 1. Solve n = 51, then compute the total number of tiles as 51^2 = 2601.

method.method_draft: Use the visual pattern as concentric odd-sized squares. The center tile is black, and each time the square expands by one layer around the center, the two diagonals add 4 new black tiles, one in each diagonal direction/corner of that layer.
